# Conductor

> Run graphs of typed Python functions.

A node is a function whose typed signature is its interface. A graph is data: its nodes, each with what is typed into it, and the edges between their outputs and inputs. A registry loads a graph into a `Graph` that reports what is wrong; a `Graph` runs, once per row wherever a list or table arrives, and a run is one value, `Run`, that pauses for a person, resumes and writes itself as JSON. The host declares its own types and nodes.

## Quick Start

One node takes a single value, the other many; that is all iteration is.

```python
registry = NodeRegistry()


@registry.node("upper")
def upper(text: str) -> str:
    return text.upper()


@registry.node("join")
def join(texts: Series[str]) -> str:
    """Joins every text it is given."""
    return "+".join(texts)


assert upper("a") == "A"  # a node is called like its function

graph = registry.load({            # a graph is data: JSON text, a mapping, or a GraphRecord
    "nodes": [{"id": "upper", "node": "upper", "many": ["text"]}, {"id": "join", "node": "join"}],
    "edges": [["upper.result", "join.texts"]],
})                                 # many: the caller gives upper.text a list, a row per item
assert graph.is_runnable, graph.problems

run = graph.run(text=["a", "b", "c"])  # by name; by address, graph.run({"upper.text": ...})
run.outputs                        # {"join.result": "A+B+C"}: what the graph returns, by address
run.results["upper"]["result"]     # ["A", "B", "C"]: ran once per value
run.results["join"]["result"]      # "A+B+C": Series[str] received every value once
```

`make_graph(*nodes, edges=None, values=None)` writes a `GraphRecord`, each node at its version and under its own id (`upper-1`, `upper-2` when one is used twice). With no `edges` the nodes form a chain: each takes its one required input no value fills from the one output before it, else `TypeError` at the call. With `edges=[("upper.result", "join.texts")]` those are every edge; nothing is matched by name. `values={"upper.text": "x"}` types values in, fixed.

## Core Concepts

### The Node Contract

`@node("id", version=, title=, description=, category=, tags=, extra=, docs=, policy=, deprecation=, compute_added_inputs=, compute_outputs=, replaces=, upgrade=)` wraps a plain function and returns a frozen, callable `NodeDefinition`; it registers nothing. `@registry.node(...)` takes the same arguments and adds the node to that registry. Only the id is required: the title defaults to the function's name in everyday words, the description to its docstring's first paragraph. `extra` is the host's own JSON about the node, kept and described, never read by conductor.

- Input: `text: str`, or `Annotated[str, Param(title=, description=, widget=, ge=, le=, max_length=, ...)]`. Without a widget an editor shows no control for it: an edge fills it, or a value set in code. A default makes it optional, and is checked against the type where it is written (`default_invalid`). A limit that can't apply to its type (`ge` on a `str`) is refused where it is written (`bound_invalid`).
- Output: `-> str` is one output named `result`, `Annotated[str, Param(title=)]` says more; a frozen dataclass is one output per field, and `Param(exclusive_group=)` on its fields marks alternatives (at most one holds a value on a row, else `invalid_output`); any other type is one value, a `dict[str, int]` included; with `compute_outputs` the function returns the outputs the hook gives as a mapping by name; `-> None` declares no outputs.
- A value can be blank. If an input's type doesn't say `| None` (`email: str | None`), the node isn't called for that row, its outputs are blank there, and `run.not_called` records the node, row and input. `Series[X]` leaves blanks out, row by row across the series inputs on one table; `Series[X | None]` keeps them. Two `Series[X]` inputs reading opposite branches of one decision would lose every row: that is `series_inputs_never_share_a_row`.
- The function returns `SKIPPED` on a branch not taken and raises `Ask(...)` when a person must answer.
- What the run supplies arrives through `FromRun[T]` parameters.
- `@node` checks the function: an `async def`, a parameter with no type, `*args`, `**kwargs` with no `compute_added_inputs`, a dataclass of outputs that isn't frozen, and a field name gone from the next version with no `Upgrade` raise `NodeDeclarationError`, with a `code`.

### Versions and Policies

A newer version names the one it replaces, a `@node` of the same id, and the decorated function is the newest. A definition is one version; the older ones hang off `replaces`.

```python
@node("greet")
def greet_v1(name: Annotated[str, Param(title="Name", widget=Textarea())]) -> str: ...

def _split_name(values: dict) -> dict:
    first, _, last = values.pop("name").partition(" ")
    return {**values, "first": first, "last": last}

@node("greet", policy=Policy(retries=2, retry_delay=0.5, attempt_timeout=10, concurrency=4), replaces=greet_v1, upgrade=Upgrade(rewrite=_split_name))
def greet(first: str, last: str) -> str: ...

assert greet.versions == (2, 1) and greet.version_of(1) is greet_v1
```

- `Policy(concurrency=1, retries=0, retry_delay=1.0, attempt_timeout=None, retry_on=(), reuse_when_inputs_match=True)`. With `concurrency` 1 and no `attempt_timeout` the node is called in order on the leg's own thread; otherwise on threads, at most `concurrency` rows at once.
- `version=` is one past the version replaced, or 1; a host whose stored graphs have their own numbers names them. `Upgrade(renamed_inputs={old: new}, renamed_outputs={old: new}, rewrite=fn)` goes beside `replaces=`; an input rename carries its value, default, `many` and edges in, an output rename the edges out of it and its columns, and `fn` takes and returns what is typed into the node, values and defaults as one map (a default stays one, anything new is a value). It is required only when a field name of the replaced version is gone.
- `registry.upgrade(record, node_id, to=None)` moves one node to a version and returns a `GraphRecord`; what it can't do is `InvalidCallError`. Loading never upgrades: a graph saved at an old version runs it.
- `Deprecation(header=, description=, alternative=, migration=)` marks a version going away (`deprecation=` on its `@node`). The `alternative` is an id for a person to read.
- A stored graph is a node too: `node("enrich", title="Enrich")(record)`, with `replaces=` and `version=` as any node. Loading a graph that uses it puts the stored graph's nodes in its place under the node's id (`enrich/upper`), on the rows the node runs on. From outside its fields go by the names it offers: the open inputs of its first nodes and the outputs nothing inside reads, bare where unique, the address on a clash (`text`, `t.text`).

### Field Hooks

```python
def operand_inputs(count: int) -> dict:          # inputs to ADD; the function takes them as **values
    return {f"value_{i}": float for i in range(count)}


def branch_outputs(names: str, value: type) -> dict:   # all the outputs; value: the type arriving on "value"
    return {name: Annotated[value, Param(exclusive_group="branches")] for name in names.split(",")}
```

Each is a plain function, given per version (`compute_added_inputs=` and `compute_outputs=` on `@node`), run when a graph is loaded, never per row. A parameter names an input and receives its typed value, the declared default included; a parameter annotated `type` receives the type arriving on that input by its edge, `Any` until one does. If a value it reads has neither a typed-in value nor a default, the hook is not called and the node's own problem says why. A hook returns `{name: type hint}`, read like a signature. A hook that raises is the problem `compute_hook_failed` on the node, never an exception. `graph.describe()` shows each node's fields as its hooks made them.

### Types

Any type pydantic can check and write as JSON travels on edges: `str`, `int`, `float`, `bool`, `date`, `datetime`, a pydantic model, a class of your own. A subtype lands where its parent is asked for, an `int` lands on a `float`. A class of your own may declare `id` (the name an editor knows it by, its class name otherwise), `display_title`, and a classmethod `accepts(source)` that lets values of another type land on it. A subclass of a builtin (`class Text(str)`) is checked as the builtin, then made one.

- `registry.types`: every type its nodes declare plus `NodeRegistry(types=[...])`, by id; one id claimed by two classes raises (`duplicate_type_id`). `registry.accepted_as(T)`: the ids a value of `T` may land on.
- `Series[X]`: many values of one type. A plain list to the node and to a type checker. `list[X]` stays one value that is a list.
- `Table[R]`, whose columns a `TypedDict` names, or bare `Table`: a whole table, a `polars.DataFrame` at run time. To a type checker it is a frame that keeps `R`: frame methods need no narrowing, a plain `polars.DataFrame` may be returned, and pyright tells two row types apart (mypy shows `R` but doesn't compare it).

### The graph record

`GraphRecord(nodes=[...], edges=[(from, to), ...])`, stored as `{"nodes": [...], "edges": [["a.result", "b.text"], ...]}`; `NodeRecord(id=, node=, version=1, values=, defaults=, many=, display=)`, empty fields left out when saved. `node` is the id of the node it uses. A node id may not contain `.`, `/` or `@` (`invalid_node_id`).

- From outside, a stored graph used as a node is one node: a caller fills `emb.text`, an author wires `emb.result`, and problems, results, `plan`, `describe()`, `decisions`, events, waiting rows and a run's `cause` name `emb`, never its inner nodes: it starts once, completes once with the outputs it offers, and says no progress of its own. Where two inner fields share a name, it offers `x.text` with `x` the inner node's id as its own record says it (for a graph embedded in it, that node and the name it offers). Its inputs stay open to the caller when edges from outside feed only some of them, and `many` on it marks one as its inner input would.
- Edges are a set, kept sorted, so two records differing only in edge order are equal. Several into one input on rows of one table gather in that table's row order; on different tables, in the order their source nodes appear in `nodes`, then the order a node declares its outputs. An edge is `node.field`, or `node.output.column` for one column of a table. An edge drawn twice is `repeated_edge`; one naming a node the graph doesn't have, at either end, is `edge_names_missing_node`.
- `values`: typed in and fixed; the graph doesn't offer that input to a caller.
- `defaults`: typed in, and the input stays open for a caller to fill. Only an open input of a first node has a caller, so a default elsewhere is `default_on_later_node`: write a value. An input takes an edge, a value or a default, never two (`value_and_edge`, `value_and_default`).
- `many`: the inputs that take a list, a row per item. On an open input of a first node the caller gives the list, and a default beside it is a list. Beside a value, on any node, the value is a list typed in: its items are a table under each row the node runs on, and the node runs once per item on each (questions typed into a node that runs per document: once per question per document). Two lists typed into one node are `two_typed_in_lists`. On an input an edge feeds it is `many_on_edge`, on a later node's open input `many_not_open`, on a `Series` input `many_on_series`.
- Nothing set: the declared default.
- `display`: the host's own, stored and never read.

### Loading

`registry.load(record)`, given a `GraphRecord`, JSON text or a mapping, never raises for a fault in the graph: each is a `Problem` (`type`, `loc`, `msg`, `ctx`) in `graph.problems`, and `graph.is_runnable` is whether there are none. The graph keeps its own copy of the definitions it resolved, so a later change to the registry doesn't reach it. A graph that embeds definitions loaded for one request loads through a registry of its own: a new `NodeRegistry`, `add_subregistry(shared)`, then `add(*definitions)`.

- `graph.inputs`: the open inputs of its first nodes (those no edge feeds), by bare name or by address where two share a name. Each has `address`, `node_id`, `input`, `many`, `required`, `default` (the record's default, else the node's) and `describe()`. An open first-node input is not a problem; a required input on a later node nothing feeds is `unbound_on_later_node`.
- `graph.outputs`: the outputs of the nodes nothing reads, by address. `graph.plan`: where each node runs, `once` or `per row of <table>`. `graph.decisions`: each node's exclusive groups and their outputs.
- `graph.describe()`: the graph as an editor draws it, as JSON: each node's fields as its hooks made them and where it runs, the inputs, the outputs, the problems. Each input of a node says how it `receives` on each row the node runs on: `one`, `per row of <table>`, `copied down from <table>` (a value from rows above) or `whole column of <table>` (a gather).
- Other codes: `unknown_node`, `unknown_version`, `unknown_input` (a value, default, `many` or edge naming an input the node lacks), `unknown_output` (an output, or a column of a table output, the node doesn't give), `type_mismatch`, `invalid_value` (a typed-in value its type refuses), `duplicate_node_id`, `cycle`, `embeds_itself`, `embedded_graph_broken` (a stored graph used as a node has problems of its own, in `ctx`), `rows_not_related`, `hook_needs_value` (a value a hook reads is not typed in), `parameter_name_invalid` (a hook gave a field a name no address can say).

### What a node returns

What a node returns is read strictly by its declared type: a value of exactly that class is taken as it is, a model may come back as a dict, but `"no"` is never a `bool`, `"12"` never an `int`, a date's text never a `date`, and `12.0` never an `int` column. A fault fails that node on that row as `invalid_output` (`ctx`: `name`, `reason`, `errors`, a table's `column`), quoting nothing of the value. A value an edge brings that its source's type doesn't settle (a limit on the input, an `int` into a `float`, a host type's own check) is read by the input as a typed-in value is, and one it refuses is `invalid_input` on the node it reached.

### Rows

A unit is a node on a row; it starts once what it reads exists, so row 1 can finish a chain while row 10 is still being made.

- An output of many values (`Series` or `Table`) makes a table named by it (`split.result`) under the row its node ran on. A row of it is its parent's key plus a number, `(0, 3)`.
- A list or a column on a single-value input runs the node per row; its outputs are columns on those rows. A value from rows above is copied down.
- A `Series[X]` or `Table` input gathers every row under the node's row. It chooses the node's row only when nothing else does: then the node runs once per row of the level right above what it gathers, and with several such inputs, above the shallowest, so none receives a list of one. A gather over a table a branch never made on that row (its maker returned `SKIPPED`) is skipped too, not called on nothing.
- A gather of a sibling table (every keyword of a document, beside each of its invoices) gathers under the row the two share. Several edges on one table into one `Series` input are read in that table's row order, one value per source per row.
- Single-value sources must lie on one path of the row tree. Rows of two different tables never meet by themselves: join them on a key in a node and wire the join (`rows_not_related`).
- Several edges into one single-value input are alternatives, each on its own branch of one decision (outputs sharing an `exclusive_group`, or what hangs off them), so a row holds at most one; otherwise `several_edges_into_one_value`. They sit on rows of one table, or `alternatives_on_different_rows`. Whole tables on opposite branches into one `Table` input are the one whose branch ran.
- Each column of a `Table[...]` output is a field at `node.output.column` (`csv.result.email`). Columns and tables wired into one `Table` input are read along one path, a parent's value copied down onto its children's rows; two columns of one name take their node's id (`name_contacts`). A `Table[R]` input receives exactly the columns `R` names, and a source that can't give one of them is `type_mismatch` at load. A table typed into a `Table` input, or given for one by a caller, is a frame or a list of records: each column `R` names is read by its own type (a date from its ISO text, a host type from its own text), other columns are left out, and a missing column or a cell its type refuses is `invalid_value` (typed in) or `invalid_input` (given), `ctx.column` naming it; `[]` is a table of no rows.
- A stored graph used as a node runs on each row its node runs on, its own reductions folding the rows under that one row.
- `SKIPPED` at a row leaves a gap in the column; above the rows it skips the node.
- `graph.run(max_rows=1000)` is a ceiling on any one table's rows (a typed-in list's are its items times the rows they go under), checked as the rows are made and before any node is called on them. Over it the run stops (`status` `stopped`) with the problem `row_ceiling` (`table`, `rows`, `max_rows`), and `run.resume(max_rows=...)` carries on with a higher one, running nothing again.

### Legs and Asking

One call of `run.resume()` is one leg. A run is its `Run`: every leg returns one, and `status` says how it ended (`complete`, `waiting`, `failed`, `stopped`, `cancelled`, `timed_out`), with `cause`, a `Problem`, for the last four. A node raises `Ask(prompt, choices=, default=, widget=)`: what is asked is what the node returns, so its return type says the answer's shape and how to ask. That row of it and what reads it wait, the rest of the graph runs on, and the leg ends `waiting`:

```python
@registry.node("approve")
def approve(invoice: str) -> bool:
    raise Ask(f"Approve {invoice}?")


approving = registry.load(make_graph(approve, values={"approve.invoice": "INV-1"}))
paused = approving.run()                                 # paused.status == "waiting"
answered = paused.answer(paused.waiting[0], True)        # raises here if wrong; no node runs
finished = answered.resume()
again = approving.load_run(finished.to_json())           # a run is JSON
```

- The return type says how to ask: `bool` a yes or no, `Literal["low", "high"]` one of its values, `str`, `int`, `float`, `date` a value, a frozen dataclass a form of one question per field (a field's default is proposed), `Table[R]` a table answered as records, `Series[X]` several, so `Series[Literal[...]]` or `Series[str]` with `choices` is a pick of several. A hook's output types ask the same way.
- `Ask` adds what only the run knows. On a node of one output: `choices=[...]` (each a value, or `Choice(id, title)` to give it a title), `default=`, `widget=` (a widget, as on `Param`). On several: `choices={output: [...]}`, `defaults={output: value}`, `widgets={output: widget}`. An `Ask` that doesn't fit the outputs (a default or choice its type refuses, a default an answer couldn't be, `SKIPPED` as a default, no choices or one offered twice, a widget with no JSON form, a name that isn't an output, choices on a table, the one-output form on several) fails the node: `invalid_ask`, with `ctx.reason`.
- Each entry of `run.waiting` is a `Waiting`: `id` (`approve@1~3fa2c0d1`: the node's id, then `@` and each number of its row, `approve` alone for a node that ran once, then `~` and a fingerprint of the question asked there), `node_id`, `row`, `prompt`, `inputs` (what the call received, as JSON) and `questions`, one per output: the field record `describe()` writes (`name`, `title`, `shape`, `type`, `schema`, `required`, ...; a lone output takes the node's title), with `choices` (`[{"id", "title"}]`, from the `Ask` or a `Literal`), `default` and `widget`.
- `run.answer(unit, value)` answers one row; `run.answer({unit_id: value, ...})` several in one call. A node of one output is answered with its value, one of several with a mapping by output name, where a question with a default, or with a blank-taking type and no choices, may be left out, and of an `exclusive_group` exactly one is answered (the others are branches not taken). Each answer is read strictly from its JSON form (`true`, not `"yes"` or `1`; `3`, not `"3"`; a date as its ISO text) and checked against its question before anything runs and returns a new run; every fault is refused at once and nothing is answered: `invalid_answer` (`ctx.waiting_id`, `ctx.reason`, `ctx.question` when it is about one), `not_waiting` for a unit not waiting, and `answer_stale` (`ctx.current`, the id waiting there now) for an id whose row holds another question since, as after `run.again` moved the rows. An id without its `~` part names the place alone and answers whatever waits there. A node that asked is not called again for that row.
- `run.to_json()` is the whole run, naming the graph it is of by `graph.fingerprint` (the record's nodes, versions, values, defaults, `many` and edges; not `display`); `graph.load_run(saved)` refuses a save of another graph as `state_of_another_graph` (an edited graph starts a new run), then reads it back and checks it against the graph: a row its makers never made, a row listed twice, a missing output or a table whose column length isn't its row count is `state_unreadable`, with `ctx.at` the `node.output` (or `node.output.column`) where. A value with no JSON form is `state_unwritable` at `to_json`, naming where too.
- A parameter typed `FromRun[T]` receives the value of `T` from `run.resume(from_run={T: value})` or `graph.run(from_run=...)`. A missing one is `from_run_missing`, at the call.

### Running again

`run.again(**changed)` runs with changed inputs, the rest as before, and reuses what it can (`run.with_inputs(**changed)` is the same run not started, to `resume()` or `stream()`, as `graph.with_inputs` is to `graph.run`): a unit whose inputs match what an earlier unit of its node received takes that result, even if its row moved, and the node isn't called. Answers are reused the same way.

```python
@registry.node("send")
def send(contact: str) -> str:
    return f"sent to {contact}"


sending = registry.load(GraphRecord(nodes=[NodeRecord(id="send", node="send", many={"contact"})]))
contacts = ["ida@a.dk", "bo@b.dk"]
first = sending.run(contact=contacts)                     # two mails
second = first.again(contact=[*contacts, "eva@c.dk"])     # one row added: one mail
```

- The key is what the unit is about to receive, by content, plus the node's version, its code (the function's own bytecode and constants, as a saved run records it), its fields and the rows it runs on. A `FromRun` value is not part of it.
- Identical rows take the earlier ones in row order, the k-th to the k-th, whatever thread finished first: a third identical row is new work, and with one identical row taken out, which earlier answer stays goes by that order, not by who answered. An answer, or a question still waiting, is reused only under the same rows above it, so two documents' identical lines keep each document's answers when the documents move. A row still waiting goes on waiting at its new row, asked nothing new.
- `again` remembers every run before it: work a run carried and didn't use is carried on, so an edit and its revert reuse the first answers.
- `run.forget("node", ...)` is a run of the same inputs that calls those nodes again (an embedding's id forgets its nodes), and a node below that then receives what it did before is reused: a host checks access again this way.
- `Policy(reuse_when_inputs_match=False)` is for a node whose result depends on the world, not its inputs (a file read by its path, today's exchange rate): `again` calls it on every row.
- `node_complete.reused_units` says how many rows were reused.

### Retries and Timeouts

Retries live on the node's `Policy`, per unit.

- Only `ExternalFailure` retries: raised by the node, or a class in `Policy.retry_on` (`external_failed`). Anything else is `execution_failed` or the node's own `NodeError` code, run once.
- Attempt `n` waits `retry_delay * 2 ** (n - 1)` and emits `node_retry`.
- `Policy.attempt_timeout` bounds one attempt: the unit fails with the code `timeout`, final; the thread is not interrupted.
- `run.resume(timeout=60)` ends the leg `timed_out`; `run.stream(cancel=asyncio.Event())` ends it `cancelled` when set, and so does leaving the loop. Either way the calls already made finish and are kept, so resuming repeats none of them.

### Errors

The classes are exported from `conductor`. What is wrong is always one record, `Problem(type, loc, msg, ctx)`: on `graph.problems`, on `node_failed` and `run.cause`, and in `InvalidCallError.errors()`. Its `type` is a stable code (see "Problem and error codes"); a node failure's `loc` is `(node_id, *row)`, a graph problem's `(node_id, field)`.

```
NodeDeclarationError    a node or registry declared wrong, at import; a TypeError, with code
InvalidCallError        a call was given what it cannot act on, every fault listed
NodeError               a node's own failure: message, code, ctx
└── ExternalFailure         retried
```

A failed unit ends the leg `failed`, its problem on `run.cause`: nothing more starts, the calls already on a thread are waited for (each as far as its `attempt_timeout`) and kept, so resuming doesn't repeat them. A call that can't be acted on raises `InvalidCallError`, whose `errors()` lists a `Problem` for every fault, and nothing changes. Running a graph with problems raises it too, listing them. A failure never quotes a value the run handled: a node's exception other than a `NodeError` goes to `logging.getLogger("conductor")` and only its class name reaches `ctx`.

### Events

`async for event in run.stream():` yields frozen models from `conductor.events`, the union `Event` on `type`; the call is checked before anything is yielded. `run_start` is always first and `run_end` always last. The leg runs on a thread of its own, so a slow node never holds the event loop. `run_end` writes only `status`: `event.run` is for the host to save, as each value already went out on its own event. An event writes itself as JSON: `event.model_dump(mode="json")`.

| Event | Carries |
|---|---|
| `node_start`, `node_skipped` | `node_id` |
| `node_progress` | `node_id`, `done`, `total` (`None` until every row exists); at most four a second per node |
| `node_complete` | `node_id`, `outputs` (as JSON, a list in row order for a node that ran per row), `not_called`, `reused_units` |
| `node_retry` | `node_id`, `row`, `attempt`, `retries`, `delay`, `cause` |
| `node_failed` | `node_id`, `cause` (a `Problem`) |
| `unit_waiting` | `unit` (a `Waiting`) |
| `run_start` | `waiting` |
| `run_end` | `status`, and `run`, which it does not write |

### Saving a graph

Records are frozen pydantic models. `GraphRecord` and `Problem` round-trip through JSON; a `Run` writes itself with `to_json()` and reads back with `graph.load_run`.

```python
record = make_graph(upper, join)
text = record.model_dump_json()
assert GraphRecord.model_validate_json(text) == record
```

### The Palette

`NodeDefinition.describe()` is a node as JSON (`id`, `version`, `versions`, `title`, `description`, `category`, `tags`, `extra`, `docs`, `deprecation`, `is_graph`, `policy`, `inputs`, `outputs`, each field with `name`, `title`, `shape`, `type`, `schema`, `required`, `default`, `widget`, `exclusive_group`). `registry.describe()` has `nodes` and `types` (each `id`, `title`, `accepted_as`).

## API Reference

Four public modules: `conductor`, `conductor.widgets`, `conductor.events` and `conductor.testing`. Each lists its names in `__all__`; import from nothing else.

### conductor

- Nodes: `node`, `NodeDefinition`, `Upgrade`, `Policy`, `Deprecation`, `Param`, `FromRun`, `Series`, `Table`
- In a node: `SKIPPED`, `Ask`, `Choice`, `NodeError`, `ExternalFailure`
- Registry: `NodeRegistry(*, category="", tags=(), extra=None, types=())` (`@registry.node`, `add(*definitions)`, `replace(definition)`, `remove(node_id)`, `add_subregistry(registry)`, `filter(predicate)`, `load(record)`, `upgrade(record, node_id, to=None)`, `in`, `[]`, `len`, iteration over the definitions, `types`, `accepted_as`, `describe`). A node entering a registry takes its defaults: tags add up, outermost first; the node's own `category` and `extra` keys win. A second node under one id raises; a subregistry is copied in when added.
- Graph: `GraphRecord`, `NodeRecord`, `make_graph`, `Graph`
- A run: `Run`, `Waiting`
- Errors: `NodeDeclarationError`, `InvalidCallError`, `Problem`, `PROBLEM_CODES`

### Running

- `graph.run(inputs=None, /, *, max_rows=None, from_run=None, timeout=None, **by_name)`: one leg from the start; its `Run`. A pause or failure is a `status`.
- `graph.with_inputs(inputs=None, /, *, max_rows=None, **by_name)`: a `Run` with the inputs checked and not started; a name it doesn't offer (`not_offered`), a required one left out (`missing_input`), one given by both its name and its address (`input_given_twice`), a value its type can't read (`invalid_input`) or a `max_rows` below 1 (`invalid_max_rows`) raises `InvalidCallError`, every fault at once.
- `run.resume(*, max_rows=None, from_run=None, timeout=None)`: the next leg. `run.stream(...)`, the same arguments and `cancel=`: the leg's events.
- `run.answer(unit, value)` or `run.answer({unit_id: value})`, `run.with_inputs(inputs=None, /, *, max_rows=None, **by_name)` (a run carrying this one's work, to resume or stream), `run.forget(*node_ids)` (a run of the same inputs that calls these nodes again, carrying the rest, to resume or stream), `run.again(...)` (the same, resumed; takes `from_run=` and `timeout=` too), `run.to_json()`, `graph.load_run(saved)`.
- `run.results`: every node's outputs so far, by node id: one value for a node that ran once, a list in row order for one that ran per row, `None` where a row has none. `run.outputs`: narrowed to `graph.outputs`, by address, on a `complete` run only (`run_not_complete` otherwise). `run.waiting`, `run.not_called`, `run.status`, `run.cause`.

### Problem and error codes

A `Problem`'s `type` comes from one table, each code with its English, and a host translates by it, filling its sentence from `ctx`. `PROBLEM_CODES` is every code conductor itself writes, for a test that pins your translations to it. A code that isn't in it is a node's own, from a `NodeError`.

### conductor.widgets

Frozen models with a `type`, and a host subclasses `Widget` for a control of its own; loading and the engine never read one. `title`, `description` and the limits of a value (`ge`, `gt`, `le`, `lt`, `multiple_of`, `min_length`, `max_length`, `pattern`) belong to the `Param`, and a value outside its limits is refused. An untitled field reads as its name in everyday words. No type has a default widget. A widget on a `Param` or an `Ask` is anything with a JSON form; one with none (a class passed bare) is `widget_not_json` at `@node`.

| Widget | Options |
|---|---|
| `TextWidget` | none |
| `Textarea` | `rows` |
| `Dropdown` | `choices` (`Choice(id, title)`, from `conductor`) |
| `NumberWidget` | `step`, `integer_only` |
| `Range` | `step` |
| `Switch` | none |
| `DatePicker` | `seed` |
| `FileUpload` | `accept`, `max_size_mb`, `multiple` |
| `ListWidget` | none |

### conductor.testing

`check_registry(registry, /, *, examples=None, expected_failures=None)` is one test a node package or host runs in CI: `assert check_registry(registry, examples={"upper": [{"text": "hi"}]}) == []`. It returns every problem at once as `Problem`s, `loc` `(node_id, version)`. A body is called only for a node given an example, once per example, through the engine as a graph of that one node; `(id, version)` keys an older version's examples, and a `FromRun` value goes in by its parameter name. The checks: `hook_failed` (a hook fails on the node's defaults and made-up values, or on an example), `needs_example` (a hook reads a required input no value can be made up for), `upgrade_broken` (an older version, moved on with `registry.upgrade`, doesn't load cleanly), `changed_its_inputs` (the body changed a value it was given; rows of a run can share one), `run_failed` (an example didn't run to the end or to a pause), `pause_untested` (the body raises `Ask`, itself or through a function it calls, and no example paused it), `example_for_no_node` and `waiver_not_needed`. `expected_failures={"id:code": "why"}` accepts a failure in the test; one that no longer fails is reported. These codes are the kit's, not in `PROBLEM_CODES`.

### conductor.events

Every event record: `Event` (the union on `type`), `RunStart`, `NodeStart`, `NodeProgress`, `NodeComplete`, `NodeSkipped`, `NodeFailed`, `NodeRetry`, `UnitWaiting`, `RunEnd`.

## Serving Runs

There is no HTTP adapter. `docs/serving-runs.md` is a page of FastAPI routes to copy into your own application: `GET /nodes`, `POST /load`, and a run you start, follow, read, answer and cancel by id. A leg is an asyncio task on the process that started it, so following and cancelling work only there.

## Project Structure

```
packages/
└── conductor/src/conductor/            __init__, widgets, events, testing: the four public modules
    ├── about/                          this document
    └── _internal/                      everything else; import nothing from here
```

## CLI Reference (this document)

```bash
python -m conductor.about                 # full text
python -m conductor.about sections        # section slugs
python -m conductor.about rows            # one section (prefix or substring)
```

Or `from conductor.about import get_content, list_sections, get_section`.
